Stays inside: this is the module's coined governing principle (a named law in the rule's own taxonomy), the maintainer block (line 43) documents it as a deliberate Antti-directed reduction ("go very lightly on the bold") down to exactly two handles across the whole 6-slide deck, and it was audited PASS at the 2026-08-02 slides stamp. Shrinking it to 5 words would break the deliberate rhetorical symmetry (general/practice) the maintainer chose; flagging a previously-audited, explicitly-directed choice on a word count alone is the shape of degrading a deliberate artefact the dispatch preamble warns against.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Heading grammar is the mood switch, and it is load-bearing.
rules_evaluated.evidence: This lecture's headings should be claims per rule 15 ("Lecture headings = claims"), but several read as noun-phrase topic labels rather than declarative claims: chunk 1 line 3 "What a skill is" (a definitional label, no assertion), chunk 4 line 19 "Two curated, one authored" (a ratio label, no verb/claim), chunk 5 line 26 "Three trust artifacts the next engineer checks" (a noun phrase with a relative clause, borderline). By contrast chunk 3 line 14 ("Your authored skill starts personal, then compounds") and chunk 6 line 32 ("The tool flags; you make the call") are genuine subject+verb claims and pass cleanly. Harm check: this rule was only added to the compendium 2026-08-15 (compendium `modified:` stamp) — after this file's last slides audit (2026-08-02, `1c765f2`) and after this file's own last content edit (`git log`: 2026-08-15) — so it has never been run against this file; the rule's own worked measurement pass was scoped to exercise files only, leaving lecture-heading conformance genuinely unverified corpus-wide. Not clearly a defect (the file predates the rule and the label style is common practice elsewhere), but a real judgment call worth surfacing rather than silently passing.
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: If maintainer wants strict conformance: recast "What a skill is" and "Two curated, one authored" as claims (e.g. a definitional or proportion assertion); "Three trust artifacts the next engineer checks" is closer and may be left as-is given its relative-clause assertion ("...checks").
